L0@P0: THE AZ ALGORITHM FOR LEAST SQUARES SYSTEMS WITH
L1@P0: A KNOWN INCOMPLETE GENERALIZED INVERSE
L2@P0: VINCENT COPPE´∗, DAAN HUYBRECHS∗, ROEL MATTHYSEN∗, AND MARCUS WEBB†
L3@P0: Abstract. We introduce an algorithm for the least squares solution of a rectangular linear system
L4@P0: Ax = b, in which A may be arbitrarily ill-conditioned. We assume that a complementary matrix Z
L5@P0: is known such that A − AZ∗A is numerically low rank. Loosely speaking, Z
L6@P0: ∗ acts like a generalized
L7@P0: inverse of A up to a numerically low rank error. We give several examples of (A, Z) combinations
L8@P0: in function approximation, where we can achieve high-order approximations in a number of nonstandard settings: the approximation of functions on domains with irregular shapes, weighted least
L9@P0: squares problems with highly skewed weights, and the spectral approximation of functions with
L10@P0: localized singularities. The algorithm is most efficient when A and Z
L11@P0: ∗ have fast matrix-vector
L12@P0: multiplication and when the numerical rank of A − AZ∗A is small.
L13@P0: Key words. Least squares problems, ill-conditioned systems, randomized linear algebra, frames,
L14@P0: low rank matrix approximation
L15@P0: AMS subject classifications. [MSC2010] Primary: 65F20, Secondary: 65F05, 68W20
L16@P0: 1. Introduction. The topic of this paper arose from the study of function approximation using frames [2, 1]. Frames are sets of functions that, unlike a basis,
L17@P0: may be redundant. This leads to improved flexibility in a variety of settings which we
L18@P0: illustrate below, but it also comes at a cost: the approximation problem is equivalent
L19@P0: to solving a linear system Ax = b that is, owing to the redundancy of the frame,
L20@P0: ill-conditioned. The central result of [2, 1] is that the function at hand can nevertheless be approximated to high accuracy via a regularized least squares approximation.
L21@P0: Thus, the linear system is rectangular, A ∈ C
L22@P0: M×N with M > N, and the cost of a
L23@P0: direct solver scales as O(MN2), where typically M is at least linear in N.
L24@P0: The particular type of frame that has received the most attention in this context
L25@P0: corresponds to Fourier extension or Fourier continuation [3, 4, 11], where a smooth
L26@P0: but non-periodic function on a domain Ω is approximated by a Fourier series on
L27@P0: a larger bounding box. Here, one can think of the redundancy as corresponding
L28@P0: to different extensions of f from Ω to the bounding box. Fast algorithms for the
L29@P0: construction of Fourier extension approximations were proposed by Lyon in [13] for
L30@P0: univariate problems and by Matthysen and Huybrechs in [14, 15] for more general
L31@P0: problems in one and two dimensions. These algorithms have the form of the proposed
L32@P0: AZ-algorithm in the special case where Z = A.
L33@P0: Thus, the AZ algorithm is a generalization of the algorithms proposed for Fourier
L34@P0: extension in [13, 14, 15]. In this paper we analyze the algorithm from the point of view
L35@P0: of linear algebra, rather than approximation theory. We supply error estimates when
L36@P0: using techniques from randomized linear algebra for the first step of the AZ algorithm
L37@P0: [10]. In contrast, the previous analysis in [14, 15] has focused exclusively on studying
L38@P0: the numerical rank of this system, in the specific setting of Fourier extension problems.
L39@P0: We characterize the scope of the algorithm and provide several examples in different
L40@P0: settings. In our analysis we focus on backward error, as the size of the residual is
L41@P0: directly related to the approximation error in the examples given.

L49@P1: There is a rich body of literature in numerical linear algebra on solution methods
L50@P1: for least squares problems. We refer the reader to the standard references [9, 12].
L51@P1: We note that direct solvers typically exhibit cubic complexity in the dimension of the
L52@P1: problem: the aim of the AZ algorithm is to reduce that complexity by exploiting the
L53@P1: specific structure of certain least squares problems. This leads to an algorithm with
L54@P1: several steps, in which existing methods for least squares problems can be used for
L55@P1: systems with lower rank. In particular we study SVD and QR based methods for step
L56@P1: 1 of the algorithm. We briefly comment on the applicability of iterative solvers for
L57@P1: least squares problems, such as LSQR [16] and LSMR [8], near the end of the paper.
L58@P1: The structure of the paper is as follows. We formulate the algorithm in §2 and
L59@P1: state some general algebraic properties. We analyze the backward error of solvers
L60@P1: for low-rank systems based on randomized SVD or randomized QR in §3. After the
L61@P1: analysis, we illustrate the algorithms with a sequence of examples: Fourier extension
L62@P1: approximation in §4, approximation using weighted bases in §5, spline-based extension
L63@P1: problems in §6 and weighted least squares problems in §7. We end the paper with
L64@P1: some concluding remarks in §8.

L86@P1: Lemma 2.1 (AZ Lemma). Let xˆ = xˆ1 + xˆ2 be output from the AZ algorithm.

L49@P1: There is a rich body of literature in numerical linear algebra on solution methods
L50@P1: for least squares problems. We refer the reader to the standard references [9, 12].
L51@P1: We note that direct solvers typically exhibit cubic complexity in the dimension of the
L52@P1: problem: the aim of the AZ algorithm is to reduce that complexity by exploiting the
L53@P1: specific structure of certain least squares problems. This leads to an algorithm with
L54@P1: several steps, in which existing methods for least squares problems can be used for
L55@P1: systems with lower rank. In particular we study SVD and QR based methods for step
L56@P1: 1 of the algorithm. We briefly comment on the applicability of iterative solvers for
L57@P1: least squares problems, such as LSQR [16] and LSMR [8], near the end of the paper.
L58@P1: The structure of the paper is as follows. We formulate the algorithm in §2 and
L59@P1: state some general algebraic properties. We analyze the backward error of solvers
L60@P1: for low-rank systems based on randomized SVD or randomized QR in §3. After the
L61@P1: analysis, we illustrate the algorithms with a sequence of examples: Fourier extension
L62@P1: approximation in §4, approximation using weighted bases in §5, spline-based extension
L63@P1: problems in §6 and weighted least squares problems in §7. We end the paper with
L64@P1: some concluding remarks in §8.

L86@P1: Lemma 2.1 (AZ Lemma). Let xˆ = xˆ1 + xˆ2 be output from the AZ algorithm.
L87@P1: Then the final residual is equal to the residual of step 1.
L88@P1: Proof. A simple expansion of the final residual yields
L89@P1: b − Axˆ = b − Axˆ1 − Axˆ2

L94@P1: overall algorithm, at least when accuracy is measured in terms of the size of the
L95@P1: residual. Furthermore, the computational cost of the algorithm is also shifted to step
L96@P1: 1, because step 2 and 3 only involve matrix-vector multiplication and addition.

L403@P5: Randomized algorithms based on matrix-vector products with random vectors
L404@P5: can compute a truncated SVD at a lower cost in case the effective numerical rank is
L405@P5: small. Algorithm 3.2 assumes that the user specifies a value R = r + p, where r is the
L406@P5: numerical rank of A and larger values of p yield higher probability of accuracy, as
L407@P5: quantified in analysis that follows.
L408@P5: The existing analysis of randomized linear algebra (see [10] and references therein)
L409@P5: focuses mostly on the accuracy of the matrix factorization. In this paper we are
L410@P5: interested mainly in bounds of the residual of Algorithm 3.2. To our knowledge, it
L411@P5: is not possible to derive residual bounds directly from the error of the factorisation,
L412@P5: so we derive the result directly using similar techniques to those in [10] for bounding
L413@P5: expectation and tail probabilities of the random matrices involved.
